cues.text:
Take the model choice from the previous
lesson and turn it into an access
decision.

Issue seventeen asks for a validator
change and a test.

Write down the two files, the working
branch,

and what you expect the assistant to
produce.

Keep production credentials and shared
deployment systems outside this task.

A manager can check the boundary by
asking the author to explain every
proposed permission against the ticket.

Try it with the test file. Reading that
file helps match the existing test
style.

Changing a pipeline falls outside the
planned work.

Sketch two boxes. The first is the
client,

such as Visual Studio Code or a CLI in
the corporate Google Cloud workspace.
The second is the model endpoint.

Draw an arrow between them and label it
with the selected code, ticket text,

and synthetic test examples that may
travel.

Have the platform owner confirm the
actual provider, endpoint,

and retention terms for the approved
setup.

The machine that runs the client tells
you one part of that story.

If you cannot name the configured
destination,

keep the real source out of the request
until the owner confirms it.

Start with the permissions to read,
edit, test, and publish.

The assistant may read the scoped
context and propose the patch on the
working branch.

The author inspects the edits and
permits the specific test run in an
approved environment.

The author publishes the branch and
opens the pull request with their own
account.

A different authorized teammate reviews
it. Read the table from bottom to top as
a check.

If you see the same identity beside
publish and final approval,

identify who will perform the
independent review before you start the
pilot.

Here is a permission prompt. The
assistant asks to download a new test
library.
Pause and ask what would justify it.

This repository already has tests in
Python's standard library,

so we have the capability needed for the
zero case.

Decline the network request and ask the
assistant to follow the existing test
style.

Then inspect the diff for package files
or dependency edits.

If your team sees a repeated request of
this kind,

the platform lead can use the examples
to clarify the task instructions or the
permission defaults.

Now follow the evidence after
publication.

In the approved remote terminal, the
reviewer uses GitHub CLI to read the

diff and the checks for pull request
forty-two.

They confirm the zero regression, see
that the checks passed,

and submit a review with their own
identity.

For the manager walkthrough, read back
that recorded decision and link it to
issue seventeen.

A passing check answers whether the test
suite ran successfully.

The review record answers who evaluated
the change.

Ask learners to point to one piece of
evidence for each question.

Make the permission decision easy to
look up.

Save the task, the approved data class,
where the assistant runs,

the actions it can take, and who handles
exceptions.

If you later evaluate Claude Code or
OpenCode in the corporate Google Cloud

workspace, check which identities grant
access to the shell, repository,
and model.

Their boundaries may differ from the
editor workflow.

Try one final exercise. A teammate asks
to connect another data source.
Who has to review that request?

In this example, the platform lead
checks the new destination and
permission before approving use.
